question: Player A controls [[Mana Vortex]] and no lands at all on the battlefield. Its third ability ("When there are no lands on the battlefield, sacrifice this enchantment") triggers and goes on the stack. Player B casts an instant that counters the triggered ability. There are still no lands anywhere. Does anything else happen?
answer: Yes. Mana Vortex's third ability is a state trigger, and the game state it checks for (no lands on the battlefield) is still true after it is countered, so it immediately triggers again and goes back on the stack. A state trigger only stops re-triggering once it has resolved, been countered, or otherwise left the stack AND the triggering condition is no longer true — being countered removes it from the stack, but does not change the board, so the very next time state triggers are checked it fires again.
key_points: Mana Vortex's third ability is a state trigger, not an ordinary triggered ability
A state trigger re-checks its condition every time it leaves the stack, including by being countered
Since no lands still exist on the battlefield, the condition is still true, so it triggers again immediately
This can repeat indefinitely as long as the countering effect is available and no lands enter
common_errors: Countering the trigger permanently stops it, since the ability has already been dealt with once
The ability cannot trigger again this turn because it already triggered once
State triggers behave like ordinary triggered abilities and do not re-fire after being countered
source: hand-authored (Claude), grounded in ruling_chunks.jsonl and the pinned CR
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude); needs human review before promotion

question: Player A controls [[Greven, Predator Captain]] (base 5/5, gets +X/+0 where X is the life they've lost this turn) and has lost no life yet this turn. Player A attacks with Greven and, from its attack trigger, sacrifices a 5/6 creature: they draw 5 cards and lose 5 life. Before this trigger finishes resolving, does Player A get a chance to gain life back in response to reduce how much Greven's power increases, and does Greven check net life change or total life lost?
answer: No response is possible: the draw and the life loss both happen as part of the same triggered ability resolving, and nothing can happen in between — no player gets priority mid-resolution to do anything, including gaining life back. Greven checks total life LOST this turn, not the net change to the life total, so even if Player A's life total had also gone up by some other amount this turn, Greven's power boost is still based on the full 5 life lost from this trigger (plus any other life lost this turn), not reduced by any life gained.
key_points: The sacrifice, the draw, and the life loss all happen while one triggered ability is resolving, so no player can act in between
Nothing can be done in response to reduce or prevent the life loss once the trigger is resolving
Greven's +X/+0 is based on total life LOST this turn, not the net change in life total
Life gained this turn does not offset or reduce the life-lost total Greven checks
common_errors: A player may respond during the trigger's resolution to gain life before the life loss is applied
Greven checks the net change in life total, so gaining life back would reduce Greven's power boost
The draw and the life loss happen as two separate events a player could respond between
source: hand-authored (Claude), grounded in ruling_chunks.jsonl and the pinned CR

question: Player A controls [[Elenda, the Dusk Rose]] (1/1, gains a +1/+1 counter whenever another creature dies) and [[Angelic Renewal]]. Another of Player A's creatures dies, putting a +1/+1 counter on Elenda (now 2/2). Later that turn, Elenda herself is dealt lethal damage and dies. Player A sacrifices Angelic Renewal to return Elenda to the battlefield. How many Vampire tokens does Elenda's death trigger create, and what are Elenda's power and toughness after Angelic Renewal returns her?
answer: Elenda's death trigger creates 2 Vampire tokens, using her power as it last existed on the battlefield (2, from the one +1/+1 counter) — not her printed power. Angelic Renewal then returns the card to the battlefield as a new object, so it comes back at its printed 1/1 with no counters, even though the trigger that made the tokens already used the higher power from before she died.
key_points: Elenda's death trigger uses her power as it last existed on the battlefield (2, from the +1/+1 counter), creating 2 Vampire tokens
Angelic Renewal returns Elenda as a new object, so she comes back at her printed 1/1 with no counters
The token count and the returned creature's stats are determined independently — one uses last-known information, the other is a fresh copy of the card
common_errors: Elenda returns to the battlefield with the +1/+1 counter still on her, since she never really left
Only 1 Vampire token is created because Elenda's printed power is 1
Angelic Renewal prevents Elenda's death trigger from happening at all, since the creature is returned
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135), not hand-invented
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A controls [[Kumano's Pupils]] ("If a creature dealt damage by this creature this turn would die, exile it instead."). It deals combat damage to Player B's creature, but before that creature would die, Player B bounces it back to hand with an instant. Player B then recasts the same card later that turn, and it dies from an unrelated source. Is it exiled, or does it go to the graveyard normally?
answer: It goes to the graveyard normally, not exiled. Returning a permanent to hand and recasting it creates a brand-new game object with no memory of its previous existence, so the newly-cast creature was never dealt damage by Kumano's Pupils — only the old object, which no longer exists, was. Kumano's Pupils' replacement effect only applies to a creature that Kumano's Pupils itself dealt damage to this turn, and this is a different object even though it's the same card.
key_points: Returning the creature to hand and recasting it makes it a new object with no memory of being dealt damage by Kumano's Pupils
Kumano's Pupils' exile replacement only applies to a creature it dealt damage to this turn, tracked per object, not per card
Since the new object was never dealt damage by Kumano's Pupils, it dies and goes to the graveyard normally
common_errors: It is still exiled, because it's the same card and Kumano's Pupils already dealt it damage this turn
Bouncing and recasting a creature does not reset which effects apply to it, since it's still the same permanent
Kumano's Pupils' effect lasts until end of turn regardless of what happens to the creature in between
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Kumano's Pupils' two existing official rulings address a different aspect (simultaneous death timing), not this bounce/recast interaction
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A controls [[Laboratory Maniac]] and casts [[Angel's Grace]] on themselves ("You can't lose the game this turn and your opponents can't win the game this turn."). Player A then empties their own library with [[Ad Nauseam]], dropping to -5 life, and later casts an instant that requires them to draw a card while their library is empty. What happens?
answer: Player A wins the game. Angel's Grace only prevents Player A from losing and prevents Player A's opponents from winning — it says nothing about Player A winning, so it does not interfere with Laboratory Maniac's replacement effect. Angel's Grace also does not stop the life loss from Ad Nauseam (it "doesn't stop loss of life from effects that say that you lose life"), so Player A's life total genuinely drops to -5, but the state-based action that would normally make them lose for having 0 or less life is suppressed this turn by Angel's Grace's "can't lose" clause. When Player A would draw from their empty library, Laboratory Maniac replaces that draw with winning the game instead, and nothing about Angel's Grace stops that.
key_points: Angel's Grace is one-directional: it stops Player A from losing and stops opponents from winning, but does not stop Player A from winning
Angel's Grace does not prevent life loss from effects that say "you lose life" (like Ad Nauseam), only changes what damage does, so Player A really does drop to -5 life
The 0-or-less-life loss (a state-based action) is what Angel's Grace's "can't lose" clause suppresses this turn, not the life total itself
Laboratory Maniac's replacement (win instead of drawing from an empty library) still applies normally, since nothing stops Player A from winning
common_errors: Angel's Grace prevents the life loss from Ad Nauseam entirely, so Player A never goes below 1 life
Since Angel's Grace says no one can win or lose this turn, Laboratory Maniac's win-the-game replacement is also prevented
Player A's life total cannot go below 1 this turn because of Angel's Grace
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135). Laboratory Maniac's own official ruling addresses the OPPOSITE direction (an OPPONENT has cast Angel's Grace) and does not itself state what happens in this self-cast scenario, which is exactly why the ruling is relevant but not sufficient alone — Angel's Grace's own asymmetric wording has to be reasoned through to reach the answer.
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A attacks with a [[Colossal Dreadmaw]] (6/6, trample) equipped with [[Basilisk Collar]] (grants deathtouch). Player B blocks with a 4/4 creature. How much combat damage does Player A assign to the blocker, and how much tramples through to Player B?
answer: Player A only has to assign 1 damage to the blocking creature, because deathtouch makes any nonzero amount of combat damage lethal for the purpose of deciding how much is required before the rest can trample through. The remaining 5 damage tramples over to Player B.
key_points: Deathtouch means any nonzero amount of combat damage is treated as lethal damage for assignment purposes
Colossal Dreadmaw only needs to assign 1 damage to the blocking creature to satisfy the lethal-damage requirement
The remaining 5 of its 6 power tramples through to the defending player
This does not require the full 4 damage the blocker's toughness would otherwise need
common_errors: The full 4 damage matching the blocker's toughness must be assigned before anything tramples through
Deathtouch and trample do not interact, so all 6 damage must go to the blocker since it is bigger than needed
Only 2 damage tramples through because the blocker still needs at least half its toughness assigned
source: hand-authored (Claude), verified no ruling exists for either card on this interaction

question: Player A controls [[Oathsworn Knight]] (0/0, enters with four +1/+1 counters; "If damage would be dealt to this creature while it has a +1/+1 counter on it, prevent that damage and remove a +1/+1 counter from it") and separately [[Polukranos, Unchained]] (0/0, enters with six +1/+1 counters; "If damage would be dealt to Polukranos while it has a +1/+1 counter on it, prevent that damage and remove that many +1/+1 counters from it"). An opponent's spell deals 4 damage to Oathsworn Knight, and a different spell deals 2 damage to Polukranos. How many +1/+1 counters does each creature have left, and what is each one's power and toughness afterward?
answer: Oathsworn Knight loses exactly ONE counter no matter how much damage was dealt — it had 4 counters, has 3 left, and is a 3/3. Polukranos loses counters EQUAL TO the amount of damage dealt — it had 6 counters, loses 2 for the 2 damage, has 4 left, and is a 4/4. The two abilities read almost identically ("prevent that damage and remove ... a +1/+1 counter" versus "remove that many +1/+1 counters") but differ in exactly the word that matters: Oathsworn Knight always removes a single counter per damage event regardless of the amount prevented, while Polukranos removes one counter per point of damage prevented.
key_points: Oathsworn Knight's ability removes exactly one counter per instance of damage prevented, regardless of how much damage that was
Polukranos, Unchained's ability removes a number of counters equal to the amount of damage that would have been dealt
Both abilities are prevention effects (615.1a): the damage never actually happens, it is replaced by the counter removal
4 damage to Oathsworn Knight (4 counters) leaves 3 counters and a 3/3; 2 damage to Polukranos (6 counters) leaves 4 counters and a 4/4
common_errors: Oathsworn Knight loses 4 counters for 4 damage, the same proportional rule as Polukranos
Polukranos loses only 1 counter regardless of the damage amount, the same flat rule as Oathsworn Knight
The damage is dealt and then counters are removed afterward as a separate cost, rather than the damage being prevented entirely
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Oathsworn Knight's official ruling states directly "removes only one counter ... not one counter per 1 damage prevented", and Polukranos's official ruling directly addresses damage exceeding its counter count, so both halves of the contrast are ruling_sufficient on their own card
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A controls no permanents except lands and a [[Glorious Anthem]], then in one turn casts [[Enchanted Evening]] ("All permanents are enchantments in addition to their other types"), [[Opalescence]] ("Each other enchantment is a creature in addition to its other types. Each enchantment has base power and toughness each equal to its mana value"), and [[Conspiracy]] (choosing the Advisor creature type as it resolves: "Each creature is the chosen type in addition to its other types"). After all three resolve, what creature type and power/toughness does a Swamp have, and what about Enchanted Evening itself (mana value 5)?
answer: The Swamp becomes a 1/1 Advisor, and Enchanted Evening becomes a 6/6 Advisor. These three effects are mutually dependent (613.8) and must be applied in the order that lets each one's own precondition already be true: Enchanted Evening first (making every permanent, including the lands and itself, an enchantment), then Opalescence (turning every enchantment into a creature with power/toughness equal to its own mana value — 0 for a land, since a land has no mana cost, and 5 for Enchanted Evening), and only then Conspiracy (which only affects creatures, so it has nothing to work with until Opalescence has already made everything a creature). Glorious Anthem's +1/+1 (a separate, non-dependent layer 7c effect) is added on top, making the 0/0 Swamp a 1/1 and the 5/5 Enchanted Evening a 6/6.
key_points: Conspiracy only affects creatures, so it depends on Opalescence having already turned permanents into creatures
Opalescence only affects enchantments, so it depends on Enchanted Evening having already made every permanent an enchantment
The dependency chain forces the application order Enchanted Evening -> Opalescence -> Conspiracy in layer 4, regardless of the order the spells were cast or resolved

A land's mana value is 0, so Opalescence gives it base power/toughness 0/0 before Glorious Anthem's +1/+1 makes it a 1/1; Enchanted Evening's own mana value is 5, giving it a 5/5 before the anthem makes it 6/6
common_errors: The three effects apply in the order their spells were cast, so Conspiracy (cast first, in some orderings) has no creatures to affect and does nothing
Timestamp order alone determines the outcome here, the way it would for effects that do not depend on one another
A land has no power or toughness to speak of even once it becomes a creature, so Opalescence and Glorious Anthem do not apply to it
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135). Opalescence's official ruling walks through the general dependency methodology in detail but for a DIFFERENT three-card combination (Opalescence + Humility + Worship) -- it teaches how to reason about dependency among type/P&T-changing effects, but does not itself state the answer for Conspiracy + Opalescence + Enchanted Evening, so the ruling is relevant without being sufficient
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player B controls [[Emrakul, the Aeons Torn]] (protection from spells that are one or more colors). Player A has 5 Swamps untapped and [[Murderous Cut]] ("Destroy target creature", a black instant... actually sorcery? treat as castable spell) in hand. Can Player A cast Murderous Cut targeting Emrakul at all?
answer: No. Murderous Cut is a black (colored) spell, and Emrakul has protection from spells that are one or more colors, so Emrakul can't legally be the target of a colored spell at all. Since Murderous Cut has no other legal target to choose (it requires exactly one target creature), there is no legal way to cast it targeting Emrakul -- the game won't even let Player A begin casting it with Emrakul as the target, rather than letting it be cast and then fizzle later.
key_points: Protection from colored spells means a permanent can't be targeted by any spell that is one or more colors, not just damage from one
Murderous Cut is a black spell, so it can never legally target a permanent with protection from colored spells
Since a legal target must be chosen at the time a spell is cast, this makes casting Murderous Cut targeting Emrakul illegal from the start, not merely a spell that later fails to resolve
This is distinct from protection only preventing damage -- protection from a quality also prevents targeting by spells and abilities with that quality
common_errors: Murderous Cut can be cast targeting Emrakul, but the destroy effect will simply fail (be prevented) when it resolves
Protection from colored spells only stops damage from colored sources, not targeting by colored spells
Emrakul can be targeted since Murderous Cut only DESTROYS rather than damages, so protection's damage-prevention clause is irrelevant either way
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); no ruling needed since 702.16b directly and completely answers this
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player B attacks with [[Prized Unicorn]] ("All creatures able to block this creature do so"). Player A's only untapped creature is a [[Silvercoat Lion]] enchanted with [[Oppressive Rays]] ("Enchanted creature can't attack or block unless its controller pays {3}"), and Player A has no mana available. Is Player A forced to block Prized Unicorn with the Silvercoat Lion?
answer: No. A creature that can't block unless its controller pays a cost is never REQUIRED to pay that cost, even to satisfy a "must block" requirement from something like Prized Unicorn -- a player can never be forced to pay a cost in order to attack or block. Since Player A has no mana and chooses not to pay {3} anyway, the Silvercoat Lion simply isn't able to block, so it doesn't count toward Prized Unicorn's requirement at all, and Player A is not required to do anything else to satisfy it.
key_points: A creature that can only block by paying a cost is never forced to pay that cost, even to satisfy a blocking requirement
Because paying the cost is optional, a creature that can't block without paying is treated as unable to block if the cost isn't paid
Prized Unicorn's "all creatures able to block do so" requirement only applies to creatures that are actually able to block, so a creature the controller chooses not to enable doesn't violate it
Player A's only creature simply doesn't block, and Prized Unicorn goes unblocked with no illegal blocking declaration
common_errors: Since Prized Unicorn forces all able creatures to block, Player A must pay {3} to enable the Silvercoat Lion and then block with it
Not blocking with the Silvercoat Lion makes the blocking declaration illegal, since a requirement is being ignored
Oppressive Rays' cost only affects attacking, not blocking, so the Lion must block regardless
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Oppressive Rays' own official ruling states this directly ("Players can't be forced to pay a cost to attack or block"), and 509.1c states the same rule generally for any cost-gated block
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player B casts [[Flame Slash]] targeting Player A's [[Atraxa, Praetors' Voice]] (4/4), then casts [[Dualcaster Mage]], whose enters-the-battlefield trigger copies Flame Slash and chooses a NEW target for the copy: Player A's [[Walking Ballista]] instead of Atraxa. The copy goes on the stack above the original Flame Slash. Before the copy resolves, Player A activates Walking Ballista's own ability twice, removing its last +1/+1 counters to ping something else, which makes Walking Ballista itself a 0/0 and it dies from a state-based action. What happens to the copy of Flame Slash, and what happens to the original?
answer: The copy of Flame Slash is removed from the stack without any effect, because its target (Walking Ballista) is no longer on the battlefield when the copy tries to resolve, and a spell whose only target is illegal is countered by the game rules. The original Flame Slash is unaffected by any of this -- it still targets Atraxa, which is a perfectly legal target, so it resolves normally afterward and deals 4 damage, destroying Atraxa. Only the copy fizzles; the original spell's fate depends entirely on its own target, not on what happens to the copy.
key_points: A copy of a spell is a separate object from the original with its own copiable values, including whichever targets were chosen for it (707.10)
Changing the copy's target to Walking Ballista (707.10c) makes the copy's legality depend only on Walking Ballista remaining a legal target, not on Atraxa
When Walking Ballista leaves the battlefield before the copy resolves, the copy has no legal target and is removed from the stack doing nothing (608.2b)
The original Flame Slash still targets Atraxa the whole time and is completely unaffected by the copy's fate; it resolves normally and deals its damage
common_errors: Since the copy of Flame Slash fizzles, the original Flame Slash is also countered because they're copies of the same spell
The original Flame Slash's target also has to be re-checked against Walking Ballista's fate since Dualcaster Mage's trigger is what created both
Walking Ballista dying prevents Dualcaster Mage's triggered ability itself from resolving, so no copy is ever created
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); no ruling addresses this specific case, but the general copy/targeting rules answer it completely
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A's [[Silvercoat Lion]] (2/2, no other abilities) is enchanted with [[Armadillo Cloak]] ("Enchanted creature gets +2/+2 and has trample. Whenever enchanted creature deals damage, you gain that much life.") and attacks unblocked for 4 combat damage. Is this the same thing as the creature having lifelink, and how much life does Player A gain?
answer: Player A gains 4 life, the same total a lifelink creature would give -- but the mechanism is different, which matters if the creature ALSO has lifelink from some other source. Armadillo Cloak's life gain is not lifelink itself; it's a separate triggered ability that goes on the stack after the damage is dealt, whereas lifelink causes the life gain to happen as a result of the damage event itself, simultaneously with the damage. If the same creature had both lifelink and Armadillo Cloak, dealing damage would gain life twice for the same damage: once immediately from lifelink, and then again from Armadillo Cloak's trigger once it resolves.
key_points: Armadillo Cloak's own text creates a normal triggered ability, not the lifelink keyword ability
A lifelink source's life gain happens simultaneously with the damage itself; Armadillo Cloak's life gain happens later, when its separate trigger resolves
In this single-source case, the two mechanisms produce the same result: 4 damage means 4 life gained
If the creature had lifelink from another source as well, both would trigger independently and the life would be gained twice for the same damage instance
common_errors: Armadillo Cloak's ability IS the lifelink keyword, just written out in full rather than as a keyword
If the creature also had lifelink, only one of the two effects would apply since they do the same thing
The life gain from Armadillo Cloak happens at the same time as the damage, exactly like lifelink
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Armadillo Cloak's own official ruling states directly it is not lifelink and stacks separately from any lifelink the creature has
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A controls [[Divine Visitation]] ("If one or more creature tokens would be created under your control, that many 4/4 white Angel creature tokens with flying and vigilance are created instead") and [[Smothering Tithe]] (creates a Treasure token when an opponent declines to pay {2} on drawing a card). Player A's opponent draws 3 cards from [[Ancestral Recall]] and declines to pay each time, creating 3 Treasure tokens. Does Divine Visitation turn these into 3 Angel tokens instead?
answer: No. Divine Visitation only replaces the creation of CREATURE tokens. A Treasure token is an artifact, not a creature, so its creation was never the kind of event Divine Visitation's replacement effect applies to in the first place -- Player A gets 3 ordinary Treasure tokens, not Angels.
key_points: Divine Visitation's replacement effect is explicitly scoped to creature token creation, by its own printed wording
A Treasure token created by Smothering Tithe is an artifact, not a creature
Since the event being replaced (a creature token being created) never happens here, Divine Visitation has nothing to apply to
The result is 3 ordinary Treasure tokens under Player A's control, with no Angels created
common_errors: Divine Visitation replaces creation of ANY token, so the Treasure tokens become Angels
Only some of the Treasure tokens become Angels, since Divine Visitation applies once per token-creation event rather than per token
Divine Visitation doesn't apply because Smothering Tithe's tokens are created by a triggered ability rather than a spell
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Divine Visitation's own official rulings address an adjacent case (a noncreature token that later becomes a creature) but not this one directly -- careful reading of both cards' own printed text settles it without needing a ruling
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A controls [[Diamond Knight]] (chose Blue as it entered: "Whenever you cast a spell of the chosen color, put a +1/+1 counter on Diamond Knight") and casts [[Glimpse of Freedom]] (a blue instant) normally from hand, then later casts it AGAIN using its Escape ability from the graveyard (exiling five other cards as the alternative cost). Does the second casting -- from the graveyard, paying an alternative cost instead of its mana cost -- still trigger Diamond Knight?
answer: Yes. Escape is simply a way of paying an alternative cost to cast a spell; the spell being cast is still a blue instant either way, regardless of which zone it was cast from or what cost was paid for it. Diamond Knight's trigger only cares about the color of the spell being cast, so both castings of Glimpse of Freedom put a +1/+1 counter on Diamond Knight -- two total.
key_points: Escape lets you cast a card from your graveyard by paying an alternative cost rather than its mana cost, but it is still casting a spell in every other respect
A spell's color and other characteristics don't change based on which zone it was cast from or what cost was paid
Diamond Knight's trigger condition is only the color of spell being cast, which is unaffected by using an alternative cost
Both castings of Glimpse of Freedom (once from hand, once escaped from the graveyard) are casts of a blue spell, so both trigger Diamond Knight
common_errors: Casting a spell via Escape from the graveyard doesn't count as "casting a spell" for triggers that care about spells being cast, since it isn't cast from hand
Diamond Knight only triggers on the first casting of a given card each game
Escape changes the spell's characteristics (since it uses an alternative cost), so it may no longer be considered blue
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); neither card's official rulings address this specific combination, but escape's own rule (casting via alternative cost is still casting normally in every other respect) settles it
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A taps Player B's [[Sejiri Merfolk]] with [[Take into Custody]], then casts [[Dream Leash]] ("You can't choose an untapped permanent as this spell's target as you cast it. You control enchanted permanent.") targeting the now-tapped Merfolk. In response, Player B casts [[Ornamental Courage]], untapping the Merfolk before Dream Leash resolves. Does Dream Leash still resolve and give Player A control of the Merfolk?
answer: Yes. Dream Leash's restriction only checks whether the permanent is tapped at the moment Dream Leash is CAST -- the Merfolk was tapped then, so it was a legal target. Once that one-time check has passed, it no longer matters if the permanent becomes untapped before Dream Leash resolves; the restriction has already been satisfied and isn't rechecked. Dream Leash resolves normally and attaches, and Player A gains control of the Merfolk even though it's untapped by the time that happens.
key_points: Dream Leash's "can't choose an untapped permanent ... as you cast it" is a one-time restriction checked only at the moment of casting, not an ongoing targeting requirement
The normal resolution-time legal-target check (whether the target still exists and is otherwise legal) does not re-examine this kind of casting-only restriction
Untapping the Merfolk in response to Dream Leash does not undo the fact that it was a legal target when chosen
Dream Leash resolves normally and gains control of the Merfolk regardless of its tapped status by the time it resolves
common_errors: Untapping the Merfolk in response makes it an illegal target, so Dream Leash is countered by the game rules for having no legal target
Dream Leash's control-changing effect only applies while the enchanted permanent remains tapped
The restriction is rechecked continuously, so Dream Leash falls off as soon as the permanent untaps
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Dream Leash's own official ruling states this directly ("checked only if you cast Dream Leash as a spell ... doesn't matter if the enchanted permanent becomes untapped")
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A controls [[Meddling Mage]], which named "Well" as it entered (the right half of the fuse card [[Alive // Well]], {3}{G} // {W}). Player A then draws Alive // Well. Can Player A cast Alive alone? Cast Well alone? Cast the card fused (both halves at once)?
answer: Player A can cast Alive alone (it wasn't named), can NOT cast Well alone (it was named directly), and can NOT cast the card fused either. A split card "has" the chosen name if either of its two names matches -- so naming just one half of a fuse card is enough to also block casting it fused, even though the other half (Alive) wasn't named. Only casting Alive by itself, without invoking fuse, is still legal.
key_points: A player naming a card with an effect like Meddling Mage may name only one of a split card's two names, never both at once
A split card counts as having the chosen name if EITHER of its two half-names matches it
Casting the card fused invokes both halves, so it counts as a spell with the chosen name even if only the other half was actually named
The unnamed half can still be cast completely normally by itself, just not as part of a fused casting
common_errors: Naming "Well" only stops casting Well by itself; the fused version is unaffected since "Alive" wasn't named
Fuse cards need both halves named separately for Meddling Mage to have any effect on them
Once one half is named, neither half can be cast at all, fused or alone
category: naming effects / split and fuse cards
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Alive // Well's own official ruling states this directly ("the player may name either half ... but not both. A split card has the chosen name if one of its two names matches")
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A's [[Reflector Mage]] enters and bounces Player B's [[Bronze Sable]] to hand ("That creature's owner can't cast spells with the same name as that creature until your next turn"). Player A also has their OWN copy of Bronze Sable in hand. Can Player A cast their Bronze Sable this same turn?
answer: Yes. Reflector Mage's restriction only applies to the OWNER of the specific creature that was bounced -- here, Player B. It says nothing about any other player, including Player A (Reflector Mage's own controller), even though Player A holds a card with the exact same name. Player A can cast their Bronze Sable freely; only Player B is locked out of casting a Bronze Sable until Player A's next turn.
key_points: Reflector Mage's restriction names a specific player -- the bounced creature's owner -- not every player or the caster of the removal effect
Owning a differently-sourced card with the same name doesn't matter; the restriction only cares about who OWNS the bounced object and who is trying to cast the named card
Player A, as Reflector Mage's controller, is never restricted by their own Reflector Mage
Only Player B, whose Bronze Sable was returned, is unable to cast a Bronze Sable until Player A's next turn
common_errors: Reflector Mage's restriction applies to any spell with that name from anyone, including its own controller
Since it's the same card name, all copies of Bronze Sable are frozen out of being cast by either player
Reflector Mage's controller can't cast the named card either, since they're the one enforcing the restriction
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Reflector Mage's own printed ability text names the specific restricted player (the bounced creature's owner) directly, so no ruling or CR citation beyond careful reading is needed
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A attacks with [[Narset, Enlightened Master]], exiling the top four cards of their library, including [[Cathartic Reunion]] ("As an additional cost to cast this spell, discard two cards"). Narset lets Player A cast noncreature cards exiled this way WITHOUT PAYING THEIR MANA COSTS. Does Player A still have to discard two cards to cast Cathartic Reunion this way?
answer: Yes. Narset's permission only waives the MANA cost -- it doesn't touch additional costs printed on the card itself. Discarding two cards is an additional cost, not part of the mana cost, so Player A must still discard two cards (and needs at least two other cards in hand to do so) even though they're paying no mana at all for the spell.
key_points: "Cast without paying its mana cost" only waives the mana cost, never any additional costs printed on the spell
Discarding two cards is Cathartic Reunion's additional cost, separate from and unaffected by its mana cost being waived
Player A must still have at least two other cards in hand to legally cast Cathartic Reunion this way
This mirrors the general rule for any alternative or cost-reduction effect: additional costs still apply unless the effect specifically says otherwise
common_errors: Since the mana cost is entirely waived by Narset, no other costs apply either and Cathartic Reunion can be cast for free
The additional discard cost is itself waived since it's part of Cathartic Reunion's total casting cost
Casting via Narset doesn't require satisfying any hand-size requirement for the discard, since it's not being cast normally
category: casting without paying mana cost / additional costs
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Narset's own official ruling states this directly ("you can pay additional costs ... If the card has any mandatory additional costs, you must pay those"), and Cathartic Reunion's own ruling confirms its discard is an additional cost
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A's [[Transcendent Master]] (a level-up creature) has been leveled up all the way to its top level (12 level counters), making it a 9/9 with lifelink and indestructible. Player B casts [[Phantasmal Image]] and copies Transcendent Master. What are the power, toughness, and abilities of Player B's copy?
answer: Player B's copy is a 3/3 with none of the upgraded abilities -- it copies Transcendent Master's PRINTED characteristics (including all of its level-up ability text at every level), but not its current level counters. Since the copy enters with zero level counters of its own, it's at its base level, with base 3/3 stats and no lifelink or indestructible, even though the original creature it copied is fully leveled up to a 9/9 with both abilities.
key_points: Copying a creature copies its printed characteristics, including a leveler's full level-up ability text at every level
Counters -- including level counters -- are NOT copiable values and are never copied along with a creature's other characteristics
The copy's own level (and therefore its power, toughness, and granted abilities) is determined by how many level counters IT has, which starts at zero
The result is a 3/3 with no lifelink or indestructible for the copy, regardless of how leveled-up the original creature being copied currently is
common_errors: The copy enters already at level 12 as well, since copying a permanent copies its current state
The copy is a 3/3 forever, since level-up abilities aren't copied at all, only the base stats
Since counters aren't copied, the copy can never be leveled up itself
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Transcendent Master's own official ruling states this directly ("the current characteristics ... and the number of level counters on it, are not [copied]. The abilities, power, and toughness of the copy will be determined based on how many level counters are on the copy")
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A activates [[Rootwater Matriarch]] ("{T}: Gain control of target creature for as long as that creature is enchanted") targeting Player B's enchanted creature. Later, Rootwater Matriarch itself leaves the battlefield (destroyed in combat). Does Player A lose control of the creature?
answer: No. The control-changing effect keeps applying for as long as the target creature remains enchanted, completely independent of whether Rootwater Matriarch itself is still on the battlefield. Once the ability resolves, the duration is tied only to the creature's own enchanted status, not to its source. Player A keeps control of the creature until every Aura falls off it, even after Rootwater Matriarch is gone.
key_points: The ability's duration ("for as long as that creature is enchanted") is a self-contained condition checked on the TARGET creature, not on Rootwater Matriarch
Once resolved, the control-changing effect no longer needs its source to remain on the battlefield to keep applying
Losing Rootwater Matriarch (its controller's permanent) has no bearing on this specific effect's duration
The effect only ends when the creature has no Auras attached to it at all, whatever else happens in the meantime
common_errors: Control reverts to Player B the moment Rootwater Matriarch leaves the battlefield, since the source of a control-change effect must remain to sustain it
The control effect is a one-time control change that isn't tied to the enchanted condition at all once granted
Rootwater Matriarch being tapped or untapped affects whether the control effect keeps applying
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Rootwater Matriarch's own official ruling states this directly ("will continue to apply even if Rootwater Matriarch has left the battlefield")
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A's [[The Wretched]] ("At end of combat, gain control of all creatures blocking this creature for as long as you control this creature") is blocked by Player B's [[Wall of Pine Needles]]. During combat, Wall of Pine Needles is dealt lethal damage and regenerates. When the end of combat trigger resolves, does Player A gain control of it?
answer: No. Regenerating a creature removes it from combat as part of the regeneration replacement effect, so by the time The Wretched's end-of-combat trigger resolves, Wall of Pine Needles is no longer blocking anything -- it isn't in combat at all anymore. The Wretched's ability only gains control of creatures that are STILL blocking it when the trigger resolves, so a regenerated creature escapes the control-changing effect entirely.
key_points: Regeneration removes the creature from combat as one of its effects, in addition to tapping it and removing damage
A creature removed from combat is no longer "blocking" anything, even though it survived the fight
The Wretched's ability checks which creatures are blocking it AS THE TRIGGER RESOLVES, at end of combat, not which ones blocked it earlier
Since Wall of Pine Needles is no longer blocking by the time the trigger resolves, it isn't affected by the control change at all
common_errors: Since Wall of Pine Needles blocked The Wretched during the fight, it's still gained even after regenerating out of combat
Regeneration only prevents destruction and doesn't affect combat status, so the creature is still considered a blocker
The Wretched's controller gains control of the creature immediately when it's dealt lethal damage, before it can regenerate
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); The Wretched's own official ruling states this directly ("Any blocking creatures that regenerated during combat will have been removed from combat... you won't be able to gain control of them")
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A controls [[Mul Daya Channelers]] (2/2, plays with the top card of their library revealed; "As long as the top card of your library is a creature card, this creature gets +3/+3. As long as the top card of your library is a land card, this creature has '{T}: Add two mana of any one color.'"). The top card of Player A's library is [[Dryad Arbor]], which is both a land card and a creature card. Does Mul Daya Channelers get the +3/+3, the mana ability, both, or neither?
answer: Both. Mul Daya Channelers has two separate, independently-checked conditional abilities -- one keyed to "the top card is a creature card" and one keyed to "the top card is a land card." These aren't exclusive modes; if a single card (like Dryad Arbor, which is both a land and a creature) satisfies both conditions at once, both bonuses apply simultaneously. Mul Daya Channelers becomes a 5/5 that can also tap for two mana of any one color.
key_points: Mul Daya Channelers has two separate conditional continuous abilities, not a single either/or choice
Each ability's condition is checked independently against the top card of the library
A card that is both a land and a creature (like Dryad Arbor) can satisfy both conditions at the same time
When both conditions are true, both effects apply together: +3/+3 AND the mana ability
common_errors: Only one bonus can apply at a time, so a card that's both types only grants the +3/+3 boost
Dryad Arbor being both types means neither condition is met cleanly, so neither ability applies
The two abilities are mutually exclusive modes chosen when Mul Daya Channelers enters the battlefield
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Mul Daya Channelers' own official ruling states this directly ("If the top card of your library is both a creature card and a land card ... Mul Daya Channelers gets both bonuses")
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A casts [[See the Truth]] ("Look at the top three cards of your library. Put one into your hand and the rest on the bottom in any order. If this spell was cast from anywhere other than your hand, put each of those cards into your hand instead.") from hand, then casts [[Twincast]] to copy it. Does the COPY of See the Truth put all three cards into Player A's hand, since it wasn't cast from hand at all?
answer: No -- the copy still only puts one card into hand, exactly like a normal cast from hand. A copy of a spell is never CAST at all (copying puts it directly onto the stack), so the copy's "if this spell was cast from anywhere other than your hand" condition is false -- there's no casting event to check the zone of. Since that condition isn't met, the copy falls back to the default: look at three, keep one, put the rest on the bottom.
key_points: A copy of a spell is never cast; it's put directly onto the stack without going through the casting process at all
See the Truth's alternate mode requires having been CAST from a zone other than hand -- a copy satisfies neither half of that (no casting event, so no zone to check)
With the condition unmet, the copy uses the spell's default, unmodified behavior: one card to hand, the rest to the bottom
This happens even though, informally, the copy exists somewhere other than a player's hand -- the rule cares about being CAST from elsewhere, not merely existing elsewhere
common_errors: The copy resolves with the alternate mode active, putting all three cards into hand, since it's clearly not being cast from hand
Copies of spells count as being cast from the stack, satisfying the "cast from anywhere other than hand" condition
Twincast's copy can't resolve See the Truth's card-selection effect at all since it was never cast
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); See the Truth's own official ruling states this directly ("if an effect copies See the Truth while it's on the stack, the copy wasn't cast at all, so you only get one of the cards")
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A activates [[Contagion Engine]]'s ability ("{4}, {T}: Proliferate twice"). Does this mean the ability resolves, and then Player A gets a second, separate opportunity later to proliferate again -- or does something else happen?
answer: Proliferating twice both happen as part of the SAME ability resolving, back to back, with no chance for anyone to act in between and no separate activation needed. Player A completes one full proliferate action (choosing permanents/players and adding a counter of each kind they already have), then immediately completes a second one -- which can target a different set of permanents and counters than the first, or the same set again (doubling up on whichever choices are repeated).
key_points: "Proliferate twice" is part of one ability's resolution, not two separate activations of the ability
No player gets priority to respond between the first and second proliferate actions
Each of the two proliferate actions is chosen independently -- the same permanents/counters can be chosen both times, or different ones
Choosing the same permanents both times simply doubles the effect on them (an extra counter of each kind, twice over)
common_errors: Proliferate twice means the ability must be activated a second time later to get its second use
Players get a chance to respond after the first proliferate action, before the second one happens
The same set of permanents and counters must be chosen for both proliferate actions
category: resolving multiple instructions in one ability
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Contagion Engine's own official ruling states this directly ("you'll complete an entire proliferate action, then you'll complete a second proliferate action ... Players can't respond between")
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A casts [[Hallowed Moonlight]] ("Until end of turn, if a creature would enter the battlefield and it wasn't cast, exile it instead"). Player B then, in the same turn: (1) casts [[Spiritual Visit]], creating a 1/1 Spirit token; (2) casts [[Reanimate]] to put a creature card from a graveyard onto the battlefield; and (3) casts a normal creature spell, [[Silvercoat Lion]]. Which of these three creatures actually ends up on the battlefield?
answer: Only the Silvercoat Lion. The Spirit token is created directly by Spiritual Visit's effect, not cast, so it's exiled the instant it would enter. The reanimated creature is put onto the battlefield directly by Reanimate's effect, not cast, so it's exiled too. The Silvercoat Lion was genuinely CAST as a creature spell, so Hallowed Moonlight's replacement doesn't apply to it at all, and it enters the battlefield normally.
key_points: Hallowed Moonlight's replacement only catches creatures ENTERING without having been cast -- it has no effect on anything that was actually cast, regardless of zone or cost paid
A token is created by its source's effect, never cast, so any creature token would-be-created this turn is exiled instead
Reanimate puts a creature directly onto the battlefield from a graveyard; that creature was never cast either, so it's exiled the same way
A creature spell that IS cast normally, like Silvercoat Lion here, is completely unaffected and enters the battlefield as usual
common_errors: Only creature tokens are affected by Hallowed Moonlight; a reanimated creature card still enters normally since it's a real card, not a token
The Silvercoat Lion is also exiled, since Hallowed Moonlight exiles every creature that enters this turn
Hallowed Moonlight only affects creatures controlled by its caster's opponents
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Hallowed Moonlight's own official ruling states this directly ("won't affect any creature that was cast ... Creature tokens are never cast")
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A sacrifices [[Burrenton Forge-Tender]], choosing [[Flametongue Kavu]] as the red source whose damage will be prevented this turn. That specific Flametongue Kavu's enters-the-battlefield trigger then deals its 4 damage, which is prevented. Later that turn, Player B casts [[Cloudshift]] on the same Flametongue Kavu, exiling and returning it, triggering its enters-the-battlefield ability again for a second 4 damage. Is this second instance of damage also prevented?
answer: No. Cloudshift returns Flametongue Kavu as a brand new game object with no connection to the one Player A chose -- even though it has the same name, same characteristics, and looks identical. Burrenton Forge-Tender's prevention effect locked onto that ONE specific object when it was chosen, and a new object is not it, so the second Flametongue Kavu's damage goes through completely unprevented.
key_points: Choosing a source for a prevention effect locks onto a specific game OBJECT, not a card name or a permanent's continuous identity
Exiling and returning a permanent (Cloudshift, blink effects generally) creates a new object with no memory of anything the old object experienced or was chosen for
The new Flametongue Kavu having the exact same name and characteristics doesn't matter -- it's a different object as far as the prevention effect is concerned
The second ETB trigger's 4 damage is fully unprevented, even though the first instance from the same-named permanent was prevented
common_errors: Since it's still "Flametongue Kavu" and the effect was chosen by name, the second damage instance is prevented too
The prevention effect lasts until end of turn regardless of what happens to the chosen permanent, including being exiled and returned
Cloudshifting a creature removes any prevention effects targeting it, but new damage triggers can't happen from the same permanent twice in one turn
category: chosen source vs. new object rule
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Burrenton Forge-Tender's own rulings address an adjacent but different case (a spell becoming a permanent), not blinking an existing chosen permanent, so this is answered by the general new-object rule rather than a specific ruling
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A controls [[Alania, Divergent Storm]] ("Whenever you cast a spell, if it's the first instant spell, the first sorcery spell, or the first Otter spell other than Alania you've cast this turn, you may have target opponent draw a card. If you do, copy that spell."). This turn, Player A has already cast one sorcery spell (which got copied by Alania). Player A now casts a SECOND sorcery spell. Does Alania trigger again and copy this one too?
answer: No. Alania's ability only triggers for the FIRST instant spell, the first sorcery spell, and the first Otter spell (other than herself) cast in a turn -- each of those three categories triggers Alania at most once per turn, regardless of how many more qualifying spells are cast afterward. Since a sorcery spell already triggered Alania earlier this turn, this second sorcery spell doesn't meet the "first sorcery spell... this turn" condition anymore, so it isn't copied.
key_points: Alania's ability keys off being the FIRST spell of a given category (instant, sorcery, or Otter) cast that turn, not every spell of that category
Once a sorcery has already triggered Alania this turn, no other sorcery can trigger it again until the next turn
The three categories (instant, sorcery, Otter) are tracked independently, so a first sorcery and a first instant could each still trigger Alania separately even in the same turn
A later, non-first sorcery spell resolves completely normally, with no copy and no opponent draw
common_errors: Alania copies every sorcery spell cast this turn, not just the first one
Once Alania has triggered once this turn (for any category), she can never trigger again that turn
The condition resets after the copy resolves, so the very next sorcery can trigger Alania again
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); answered directly by Alania's own printed condition ("the first ... spell ... you've cast this turn"), no ruling or CR citation needed beyond reading it carefully
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A casts [[Unleash the Inferno]] ("deals 7 damage to target creature or planeswalker. When it deals excess damage this way, destroy target artifact or enchantment an opponent controls with mana value less than or equal to that amount of excess damage") targeting Player B's [[Stone Golem]] (4 toughness). Player B also controls a 3-mana-value artifact and a 4-mana-value artifact. Which artifact, if any, can Unleash the Inferno destroy?
answer: Only the 3-mana-value artifact. Unleash the Inferno deals 7 damage to a 4-toughness creature, so the excess is 7 minus 4, or 3. The linked ability can only destroy an artifact or enchantment with mana value 3 or less, so the 3-mana-value artifact is a legal target and gets destroyed, while the 4-mana-value artifact is not a legal target at all and is untouched.
key_points: Excess damage to a creature is the amount dealt beyond what was needed to be lethal -- here, 7 damage minus 4 toughness equals 3 excess
The destroy effect's target must have a mana value no greater than the amount of excess damage actually dealt
An artifact with a HIGHER mana value than the excess damage is simply not a legal target for the ability
A permanent can never be dealt zero excess damage -- if the excess were exactly zero, the second ability wouldn't have a legal amount to work with at all
common_errors: Either artifact can be chosen, since the full 7 damage is what matters, not the excess over lethal
The 4-mana-value artifact can be destroyed too, since 4 is close enough to 3 excess damage
Excess damage is calculated from the creature's power, not its toughness
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Unleash the Inferno's own official ruling defines excess damage directly ("greater than lethal damage... usually toughness") and confirms the mana-value threshold mechanism
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion

question: Player A's [[Thorn Elemental]] (7/7, "You may have this creature assign its combat damage as though it weren't blocked") attacks and is blocked by Player B's [[Grizzly Bears]]. Player A chooses to use this ability. How much damage does Grizzly Bears take, and how much does Player B take?
answer: Grizzly Bears takes 0 damage, and Player B takes all 7. Thorn Elemental's ability is an all-or-nothing choice: either assign all of its combat damage to the blocking creature as normal, or assign ALL of it to the player or planeswalker it's attacking, with no way to split the damage between them the way trample would allow.
key_points: Thorn Elemental's ability lets its controller choose to assign ALL combat damage to the defending player/planeswalker instead of the blocker, once per combat
This is an all-or-nothing choice, unlike trample -- there's no way to assign some damage to the blocker and the rest to the player
Choosing this option means the blocking creature (Grizzly Bears) takes zero combat damage from Thorn Elemental
The full 7 damage goes to the defending player even though Thorn Elemental was blocked
common_errors: Thorn Elemental can split its damage between the blocker and the player, similar to a trampling creature
The blocker still takes some damage even when this ability is used, since it did block the attacker
Using this ability requires the blocker to first be dealt lethal damage before excess damage can go to the player
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Thorn Elemental's own official ruling states this directly ("you choose whether you want to assign all damage to blocking creatures, or if you want to assign all of it to the player ... You can't split the damage assignment between them")
rubric_source: hand-authored (Claude) from a verified XMage test; needs human review before promotion
